editor_spans.body: The Derby headquarters is framed as a fresh start, but it is the latest chapter of a long reversal. Great British Railways was first proposed by a previous government after the post-privatisation franchise model visibly failed. Its building at Becketwell will not be finished until spring 2029, so an organisation first announced in 2021 will have waited most of a decade for a permanent home. The slow pace says more about how hard it is to unwind thirty years of fragmented rail structures than any ribbon-cutting does.

The figures are worth reading closely. The site will hold up to 450 GBR staff, and many of those posts are likely to be relocations from existing bodies rather than new work. That is why the 'hundreds of jobs' line is softer than it sounds. The more telling number is buried deeper: fewer than 7% of the railway's workforce is under 25. That is the industry's real structural risk, a skills cliff built up over decades of underinvestment in training. Up to 600 apprentices over four years is a modest answer to it.

The fare freeze is credited to public ownership. But fares on regulated routes were always set by government policy, so a freeze is a political choice that could have been made under any ownership model. The test of renationalisation will be reliability and cost over years, not the first round of announcements.

Behind the 'rock-solid' language on Ukraine sits a strategic dependence. London 'fully supports US-led efforts' and welcomes an energy ceasefire that Washington announced. Days later it is complaining that Russia has ignored that ceasefire. Britain and Europe are reacting to a peace process whose terms are set elsewhere.

The sums also deserve scrutiny next to the rhetoric of going 'further and faster'. The acceleration amounts to £10 million of a £45 million package. Most of the headline LMM commitment is spread over four years. Ministers have been asked to 'draw up' further packages, which means they do not yet exist.

Britain's most distinctive lever may not be missiles at all. It is the maritime ban on Russian LNG, built on London's dominance of shipping and insurance services, a legacy of centuries of commercial history. That only works if partners follow, which is why the Chancellor and the Foreign Secretary are lobbying abroad. The government also openly worries about the energy-price fallout at home, and there is a tension between squeezing Russian energy revenues and protecting the cost of living.

The most consequential line in the Commons statement is not about the 20 November summit. It is the Prime Minister's call for a 'serious dialogue' about Britain's long-term relationship with the EU. Ten years after the referendum, the case is being rebuilt from the bottom up: salmon document checks, seed potato bans, export health certificates. Ministers are betting that the accumulated friction costs to farmers and small firms will shift opinion where abstract arguments did not.
The promise that 'the public will be the boss' is a careful hedge. The government is opening a door it does not yet dare to walk through.

The offer to Holyrood is Greater Manchester's metro-mayor model being exported by a Prime Minister who built his career on it. Framing the Scottish Government as over-centralised turns devolution's logic back on the devolved administration itself. Routing regional empowerment through No10 North and the Scotland Office will inevitably look, to Edinburgh, like Westminster reaching past Holyrood into Scotland's regions.
